name: DeepSpeed-MII (DeepSpeed-Inference)
notable_features: The 'apply the right inference path automatically' idea, and this is the record for it: based on model architecture, model size, batch size and available hardware, MII chooses the inference implementation itself. Most engines make you choose; this one picks
Four named throughput technologies in the README: blocked KV caching, continuous batching, Dynamic SplitFuse, and high-performance CUDA kernels

Dynamic SplitFuse is the distinctive contribution - fusing the prefill and decode phases' kernel launches so a mixed batch does not stall between the two shapes of work. This predates vLLM's chunked-prefill framing of the same problem by a couple of years
DeepSpeed-FastGen (2023/11 blog) is where the performance analysis lives, including Mixtral, Phi-2 and Falcon support (2024/01)
Non-persistent pipelines for trying it out without standing up a server
Pre-compiled python wheels covering most of the custom kernels, explicitly to avoid the long compile times the README says many projects in this space require
Legacy section retained in the README: DeepFusion for Transformers and multi-GPU inference with tensor-slicing, from the low-latency era
Was Microsoft's project before the org move; github.com/microsoft/DeepSpeed-MII still resolves via redirect
2114 stars, Apache-2.0, v0.3.3 released 2025-03-25, last push 2025-06-30
hardware_caveats: EFFECTIVELY WOUND DOWN. Last push 2025-06-30, last release v0.3.3 from 2025-03-25, and the newest news item in the README is dated 2024/01. Marked deprecated on that evidence - there is no deprecation notice, the repo simply stopped
The README has no 'successor' line and no archive banner, so anyone arriving cold has no signal that this is finished. The signal is only in the dates

CUDA only in practice. Four of the four named technologies are CUDA-kernel technologies, Dynamic SplitFuse is a CUDA launch-fusion technique, and the repo's language breakdown is Python only with no C++/CUDA extension source in-tree (the kernels live in DeepSpeed itself). No ROCm, Metal, Vulkan or CPU-server path is documented for the text-generation stack

The kernels live in DeepSpeed, not in MII, so the coupling is to DeepSpeed's release cadence and its compile requirements. The pre-compiled wheels trade that coupling for a stale-binary risk: a wheel that does not match your Torch/CUDA versions is a hard failure

Automatic optimisation cuts both ways. Because MII chooses the path for you, the interesting knob - which inference implementation is running - is not directly exposed, which makes it hard to reason about why performance differs from what you expect

SplitFuse is now largely subsumed. vLLM's chunked prefill and SGLang's overlap scheduling address the same prefill/decode interference, and they are the paths with community, hardware-plugin and format support
Historical importance exceeds current utility: this is the clearest pre-vLLM statement of continuous batching plus KV blocking plus phase fusion as one system, published as a blog rather than a paper
best_for: Reading the clearest pre-vLLM articulation of continuous batching + blocked KV + prefill/decode fusion as a single design - the DeepSpeed-FastGen blog is the primary source
Understanding Dynamic SplitFuse, which named the problem vLLM's chunked prefill and SGLang's overlap scheduling later solved and popularised
Studying automatic path selection from model and hardware characteristics, a design few engines attempt
Historical reference for the 2022-2024 generation of high-throughput LLM serving
avoid_for: Anything new - the project has been effectively wound down since mid-2025
Non-CUDA hardware; there is no ROCm or CPU-server story for the text-generation stack
Production deployments that need a maintained release train or an explicit choice of inference backend
New-format support: safetensors-era quantisation paths landed in vLLM/SGLang, not here
notes: The pre-vLLM high-throughput engine that the brief's 'historically-influential' category is really about. Its legacy section (DeepFusion, tensor-slicing multi-GPU) and its four named technologies make it the best single artifact for understanding where continuous batching came from. Deprecated status is based on dates (last push 2025-06-30, last release 2025-03-25, newest README news 2024/01) rather than an official notice. Org note: the repo moved from microsoft/ to deepspeedai/; the old URL still resolves by redirect.
